title: Code erodes as agents build on their own work
summary: Each agent change on top of earlier agent changes adds a little duplication and complexity. Better prompts set a better starting point but don't stop the slide; only refactoring and review do. Whether newer models maintain code better is disputed: one measure shows fast gains, another the same decay across model tiers.

title: You can't tell from a task how well the agent will do
summary: Agents fail on tasks unlike what they were trained on, not on tasks that look hard. A task that seems easy can fail and a hard one succeed, so judge from real results on your work.

title: Every line in the context file costs money
summary: Agents do follow context-file instructions, which means each mention of a tool or step gets acted on, every task. Extra instructions raise spend even when they don't help, and whether context files help at all is disputed: one source finds time saved, another no gain in success.

title: Agents act on outdated facts
summary: When a fact changes, agents often keep using the old version from memory or context files. Updated decisions need to replace, not sit beside, the old ones. Building the update into every task may keep notes current, but even its advocates still trim them by hand.

title: Agreeable answers mislead without being wrong
summary: Assistants tend to agree with the person asking and pick facts that support them. Each statement can be true while the overall picture is skewed, and people rate these answers as more objective.

title: Review load lands on senior engineers
summary: PR volume has grown several times over while reviewer numbers haven't, so the extra review falls on the few people trusted to approve. Some teams move trust into tests and production checks and auto-merge part of their changes instead; whether that holds up isn't known yet.

title: People follow AI advice they know is wrong
summary: Even reviewers who spot a flaw in an AI recommendation often go along with it. Spotting a problem isn't enough; reviewers need the time and the authority to reject.

title: Nobody knows how often agents leak secrets
summary: The risk of agents exposing credentials is clear from how they work, but there are no measured leak rates. Plan for it as you would any likely risk: keep secrets out of reach. (OWASP LLM02, LLM07)

title: Prompt injection has no proven fix
summary: The one architecture shown to block most injection attacks has only been tested by its own authors, who say the problem isn't solved, and a guardrail that stops most attacks still fails by security standards. Limit what an agent can do rather than hoping it can't be tricked; whether an agent should ever approve its own change is still open. (OWASP LLM01)

title: Test loops fix the code, not a misread requirement
summary: Letting an agent iterate against tests repairs edge cases and type errors, but if it misunderstood what was asked, it stays misunderstood. Only a person checking intent catches that.

title: Supervising agents needs the skills agents erode
summary: Checking agent code well takes hands-on coding skill, and relying on agents can wear that skill down. Without deliberate practice, a team loses the ability to review what it ships. Nobody knows yet whether the loss reverses or how to measure it.

title: Juniors ask the model instead of colleagues
summary: Most of a junior engineer's questions now go to an assistant rather than a teammate, and entry-level hiring is shrinking. The quick answer replaces the conversation where they would have learned how the team works, and nobody yet knows how juniors will grow into seniors.

title: Shared agent memory behaves like a shared database
summary: Team context files, skills and memory stores can leak data, go stale, hide contradictions and lose track of who wrote what. Nobody has settled how conflicting writes should be handled.

title: Pairing with AI isn't the same as pairing with a person
summary: Results on pairing with an assistant disagree, and some show lower quality than a human pair. It also skips the knowledge sharing that pairing exists for.

title: Test-first results may not hold on current models
summary: The evidence that writing tests first helps agents comes from one language and from models that predate current ones, and nobody has re-checked it. Vague requirements, where test-first is said to help most as a way of thinking, haven't been tried with agents.

title: Nobody agrees what the human bottleneck is now
summary: With agents writing the code, practitioners disagree on whether verification, judgement or understanding becomes the constraint. Each position rests on one person's experience or opinion.

title: Strong engineering foundations may not protect you
summary: One industry survey says good practices partly shield teams from AI's downsides; telemetry across many companies finds no outcome protected. Don't assume a mature process makes agent adoption safe; watch your own delivery numbers.

title: Nobody knows how much to specify up front
summary: Giving agents more tests up front helped only to a point, and agents that designed before coding did better, so heavy spec-first work risks repeating waterfall. Others argue the spec is the lasting artifact and should be executable; the evidence doesn't settle it.

title: Planning and execution prompts may need different detail
summary: One practitioner argues for goals-only planning prompts and fully detailed execution prompts. It is an opinion nobody has tested.

title: Fresh or continued context in agent loops is unsettled
summary: Some loops reset the agent's context every iteration; one comparison on a single task found continuing did better for the cost. Nobody has compared them on real work.

title: Nobody knows if multi-agent orchestration scales
summary: Adding agents may run into the same coordination cost as adding people to a late project (Brooks's Law). No controlled comparison exists yet.

title: It's unclear how much of a system a team must understand
summary: One view holds that a team's understanding of its system can't be rebuilt from documents once lost; another says most engineers work fine with a partial picture. With agents writing more of the code, the answer decides how much understanding a team has to keep.
